source_text: Omnibus ergo delictis seu carne seu spiritu seu facto seu voluntate commissis qui poenam per iudicium destinavit, idem et veniam per paenitentiam spopondit, dicens ad populum, Paenitere, et salvum faciam te. Et iterum, Vivo, inquit, dominus, et paenitentiam malo quam mortem. Ergo paenitentia vita est, cum praeponitur morti. Eam tu peccator, mei similis (immo me minor, ego enim praestantiam in delictis meam agnosco), ita invade, ita amplexare, ut naufragus alicuius tabulae fidem. Haec te peccatorum fluctibus mersum prolevabit et in portum divinae clementiae protelabit. Rape occasionem inopinatae felicitatis, ut ille tu nihil quondam penes deum nisi stilla situlae et areae pulvis et vasculum figuli arbor exinde fias illa quae penes aquas seritur et in foliis perennat et tempore suo fructus agit, quae non ignem, non securem videbit. Paeniteat errorum reperta veritate, paeniteat amasse quae deus non amat, quando ne nos quidem ipsi servulis nostris ea quibus offendimur non odisse permittimus. Obsequii enim ratio in similitudine animorum constituta est. De bono paenitentiae enumerando diffusa et pro hoc magno eloquio committenda materia est Nos vero pro nostris angustiis unum inculcamus, bonum atque optimum esse quod deus praecipit. Audaciam existimo de bono divini praecepti disputare. Neque enim quia bonum est, idcirco auscultare debemus, sed quia deus praecepit. Ad exhibitionem obsequii prior est maiestas divinae potestatis, prior est auctoritas imperantis quam utilitas servientis. Bonum est paenitere, an non? Quid revolvis? deus praecipit. At enim ille non praecipit tantum, sed etiam hortatur. Invitat praemio, salute; iurans etiam, Vivo, dicens, cupit credi sibi. O beatos nos, quorum causa deus iurat! O miserrimos, si nec iuranti domino credimus! Quod igitur deus tantopere commendat, quod etiam humano more sub deieratione testatur, summa utique gravitate et aggredi et custodire debemus, ut in asseveratione divinae gratiae permanentes in fructu quoque eius et emolumento proinde perseverare possimus.
orientation: Tertullian is addressing the sinner directly, arguing that the same God who appointed punishment for sins has also promised forgiveness through repentance.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore to all sins, whether committed by flesh or by spirit, whether by deed or by will, he who has destined punishment through judgment, the same one has also promised forgiveness through repentance, saying to the people, Repent, and I will save you. And again, I live, says the Lord, and I prefer repentance to death. Therefore repentance is life, when it is preferred to death. You, sinner, like me (indeed less than me, for I acknowledge my own preeminence in sins), seize it, embrace it, as a shipwrecked man seizes the trustworthiness of some plank. This will lift you up when you are sunk in the waves of sins and will carry you into the harbor of divine mercy. Seize the opportunity of unexpected happiness, so that you, who once were nothing before God except a drop of a bucket and dust of a threshing floor and a little vessel of a potter, may from then on become that tree which is planted beside waters and remains green in its leaves and produces fruit in its season, which will not see fire, will not see the axe. Let him repent of his errors when the truth has been found, let him repent of having loved what God does not love, since not even we ourselves permit our own slaves to not hate the things by which we are offended. For the principle of obedience is established in the likeness of minds. On the good of repentance, a diffuse matter must be committed to enumeration and for this to great eloquence. But we, for our narrow limits, press one thing: that what God commands is good and best. I consider it audacity to dispute about the goodness of a divine command. For it is not because it is good that we ought to obey, but because God has commanded. For the display of obedience, the majesty of divine power is prior, the authority of the one commanding is prior to the usefulness of the one serving. Is it good to repent, or not? Why do you turn it over? God commands. But indeed he does not only command, but also urges. He invites with a reward, with salvation; swearing even, saying, I live, he desires to be believed. O blessed we, for whose cause God swears! O most wretched, if we do not believe the Lord even when he swears! Therefore what God so greatly commends, what he also testifies in human fashion under an oath, we ought with the utmost seriousness both to undertake and to guard, so that, remaining in the assertion of divine grace, we may likewise be able to persevere in its fruit and benefit as well.

choices.why: Glossary term; must use 'repentance' and never 'penance' or 'penitence'.

choices.why: Literal rendering preserves the metaphor of clinging to a plank's reliability; 'fidem' as 'trustworthiness' keeps the abstract noun force.

pass_b_english: So the same God who has appointed punishment by judgment for every sin, whether of flesh or spirit, whether in act or in will, has also promised forgiveness through repentance. He says to his people: "Repent, and I will save you." And again he says: "As I live, says the Lord, I desire repentance rather than death." Repentance, then, is life, since it is preferred to death.

You, sinner like me, no, less than me, for I acknowledge my own preeminence in sins, seize it and embrace it as a shipwrecked man seizes the solidity of some plank. It will lift you up when you are drowning in the waves of sin and carry you forward into the harbor of divine mercy. Snatch the chance of unexpected happiness: you who were once nothing before God but a drop of a bucket, dust of the threshing floor, a potter's little vessel, become from then on that tree which is planted by the waters, remains green in its leaves, and bears fruit in its season, which will see neither fire nor axe. Let repentance follow the discovery of truth after error; let it repent of having loved what God does not love, since we ourselves do not even allow our own servants to fail to hate the things that offend us. For the principle of obedience is established in likeness of minds.

The good of repentance could be set out at length, and this great theme deserves eloquence. But I, within my narrow limits, press one point upon you: what God commands is good and best. I consider it audacity to debate the goodness of a divine command. We should not obey because it is good, but because God has commanded it. For the performance of obedience, the majesty of divine power comes first; the authority of the one who commands comes before the advantage of the one who serves.

Is it good to repent or not? Why do you turn it over? God commands it. And he does not merely command, he also urges. He invites with a reward: salvation. Even swearing, saying "As I live," he desires to be believed. O how blessed we are, for whose sake God swears! O how wretched, if we do not believe the Lord even when he swears! What God so earnestly commends, what he testifies even in human fashion under an oath, we must undertake and guard with the utmost seriousness, so that as we remain in the assertion of divine grace we may likewise persevere in its fruit and benefit.

last_rejected.quote: I acknowledge my own preeminence in sins
last_rejected.source_quote: ego enim praestantiam in delictis meam agnosco
last_rejected.why: 'praestantia' here means being foremost/excelling in sins, not preeminence as superiority.
last_rejected.fix: for I acknowledge that I excel in my own sins
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'praestantiam...agnosco' = I acknowledge my excellence/foremostness in sins; 'preeminence' conveys same sense

last_rejected.quote: "As I live, says the Lord, I desire repentance rather than death" (Ezekiel 33:11)
last_rejected.why: The cited verse does not contain that wording; Ezekiel 33:11 speaks of not putting to death and turning away sin, not a desire for repentance.
last_rejected.fix: Remove the citation or quote the verse accurately, e.g., "As I live, says the Lord, I will not put you to death but will turn away from you the sin" (Ezekiel 33:11).
last_rejected.ruling: Ezekiel 33:11 'I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked...turn and live' matches 'paenitentiam malo quam mortem' (prefer repentance to death).

problems.quote: seize it and embrace it as a shipwrecked man seizes the trustworthiness of some plank
problems.why: 'Trustworthiness' is an odd modern abstraction; the Latin likely means 'reliability' or simply 'solidity' of a plank.
problems.fix: Render as 'the solidity of some plank' or 'any plank that holds.'

fixed: Changed 'trustworthiness' to 'solidity' for 'fidem' in the plank simile, since the Latin means the reliability or solidity of the plank, not an abstract trustworthiness.
